The prose of the quote is there word for word: 'The first syllable of a word seems to be the one that is slightly stressed. It is difficult to hear and at one stage we thought that we heard stress on different syllables in different words, though we no longer do. Stress in Elopi is force and slightly higher pitch, perhaps also very slight lengthening of the syllable.' followed by the four template examples S /bE/ 'fire', SW /ada/ 'foot', SWW /hokEdi/ 'turtle', SWWW /hat(h)Ebada/ 'white' (typewriter epsilon; the first reader's IPA rendering and run-together layout are the only differences, hence 'minor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak, non-contrastive word stress on the first syllable of the word (S, SW, SWW, SWWW patterns), in a language with five lexical tones (high, mid, low, rise, fall); stress cues are intensity, slightly raised pitch and possibly slight lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the S/W templates show a single initial stress with all following syllables weak up to four syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None; authors note stress is hard to hear and that they earlier thought it fell on different syllables in different words but abandoned that view (p.22); p.20 adds that early on stress was misheard as an additional 4-3 rise tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, stated over isolated words of one to four syllables; the paper is a tentative 'first phonology' (draft working paper) based on fieldwork 1981-1988 mainly in Kodesi village. Tone (sec. 6) is the contrastive prosodic system; Clouse 1997:160 independently states stress has not been found contrastive in any Lakes Plain language.
new_statements.identity_note: Source calls the language 'Elopi' (speakers: Tilopi; older name Dou), western Lakes Plain along the Tariku (Rouffaer) River, data mainly from Kodesi (Kordesi) village 1981-1988, c.700 speakers; this is the same language as Glottolog edop1238 / ISO dbf Edopi (SIL archive files it under dbf). No dialect subdivision given; authors remark idiolectal variation is high.

sources.note: Sec. 7 STRESS (printed p.22 / PDF p.23): 'The first syllable of a word seems to be the one that is slightly stressed'; hard to hear; realised as force + slightly higher pitch, perhaps slight lengthening; examples S /bE/ 'fire', SW /ada/ 'foot', SWW /hokEdi/ 'turtle', SWWW /hathEbada/ 'white'. Sec. 6 TONE (pp.19-21): five tones (high, mid, low, rise, fall); p.20 notes that early on stress was misheard as an extra rise tone. Sec. 8 (p.23) refers to stressed vs unstressed syllables; sec. 5 (p.16) gives an unstressed-syllable allophone of /a/.
